AI Audio

Turn your sound on for this one

Sound is air moving back and forth

When something makes a sound, it shakes the air. A guitar string, a speaker, or your vocal cords push the air and pull it back, over and over. Those pushes travel to your ear like ripples in a pond.

How fast the air shakes is the pitch. More shakes per second sounds higher. This is measured in hertz (Hz), which just means "times per second". How hard it shakes is the loudness.

People hear from about 20 Hz, a deep rumble, up to about 20,000 Hz, a thin whine. The top end drops as we get older, and many adults can't hear much above 15,000 Hz.

Try it: press Play, then move the slider. Push the pitch up past 15,000 Hz and see who in the room can still hear it.

Real sounds are many waves added together

A pure tone like that is rare in real life. When a flute, a violin or a person sings a note, you hear the main pitch plus a stack of quieter, higher waves on top of it. These are called overtones.

The overtones sit at 2, 3, 4 times the main pitch, and so on. How loud each overtone is gives a sound its character. That's how you can tell a flute from a trumpet, even when they play exactly the same note.

Your voice works the same way. The shape of your mouth changes which overtones are loud. That's the difference between "ee" and "oo".

Try it: press Play and switch between the sounds. The pitch stays the same the whole time. Only the mix of overtones changes.

main×2×3×4×5×6×7×8

A recording is a long list of numbers

Inside a microphone is a thin sheet that moves with the air, the same way your eardrum does. The computer measures where the sheet is, thousands of times every second, and writes each measurement down as a number.

Music on a CD is measured 44,100 times a second. So a three-minute song is about 8 million numbers, for each ear. To play it back, the numbers move the speaker, and the speaker moves the air.

If you measure less often, you miss the fast wiggles, which are the high sounds. The voice gets dull and muffled. Phone calls used to be measured just 8,000 times a second, which is why they sounded the way they did.

Try it: pick fewer measurements per second and press Play.

A picture of sound

Looking at the wave doesn't tell you much. It's just a squiggle. So computers usually turn sound into a picture first, called a spectrogram.

Time goes left to right. Pitch goes bottom to top: low sounds at the bottom, high sounds at the top. The darker a spot, the louder that pitch is at that moment.

Each sound leaves its own pattern. A whistle is a thin line. A "sss" sound is a haze up high. Vowels are stacks of stripes, which are the overtones.

Once sound is a picture, AI can learn from it the same way it learns from photos.

Try it: press "Use my mic", then whistle, hum, say "sssss", then "eeee" and "oooo". Or play the voicemail or the song.

Speech to text: from picture to words

To turn speech into text, the AI cuts the spectrogram into thin slices, each a few hundredths of a second long. Each slice becomes a list of numbers.

Then a transformer, the same kind of model behind ChatGPT, reads the slices and writes out the words, token by token. It works a lot like translating, only from sound into text.

Whisper, a well-known speech model from OpenAI, learned from 680,000 hours of recordings that came with transcripts. Listening to all of it, day and night, would take you 77 years.

Try it: press Play to see the idea. Then press "Start listening" and talk. Watch how a word can change once the model hears what comes after it.

Your words will appear here.

When words sound the same, the sentence decides

Plenty of phrases sound almost exactly alike, like "ice cream" and "I scream". From the sound alone, the model can't tell them apart.

So it does what a language model does: it uses the rest of the sentence.

This is also why speech to text struggles with names it has rarely seen, like an unusual street or your cousin's name.

Try it: pick a sentence and watch the guesses change.

It hears how you said it, not just what

Older voice assistants turned your voice into text and threw the sound away. The words made it through, but your tone of voice didn't.

The newest models listen to the sound itself. They can tell if you're joking, upset or in a hurry. They can hear a laugh, a sigh, a dog barking in the background, or two different people talking.

On the right are two recordings with exactly the same words. An AI model was asked how the speaker feels: first with only the words, then with the recording.

Try it: play both recordings and decide for yourself. Then show what the model said.

"Oh, you got the job in Denver. That's amazing. I'm so happy for you."

How computers used to talk

Computers have been able to talk for decades. The older way was to record a person saying thousands of tiny pieces of sound, then glue the right pieces together. Some systems used hand-written rules for how each letter should sound.

It works, but you can often hear the joins. Every sentence tends to come out with the same flat rhythm, because the computer doesn't know what it's saying.

Your device has a built-in voice too. Here's the voicemail from the start, read by your device and by AI.

Try it: play both and compare.

Making sound token by token

The new way of making speech uses the same idea as chatbots. First, a program called a codec learns to squeeze sound into tokens. Each token stands for a tiny moment of sound, a few hundredths of a second.

Then a language model learns to predict the next sound token, the same way it predicts the next word. Give it text, and it writes out sound tokens. The codec turns those back into a wave you can hear.

Because the model has listened to so much real speech, it picked up where people pause, which words they stress, and how a question goes up at the end. Nobody wrote those rules.

Try it: press Play. Each sound token lights up as it is turned back into sound.

Text tokens in
↓Voice model↓
Sound tokens out

Telling the voice how to say it

New AI voices take directions, like an actor. In many voice tools you write a note in square brackets right in the text: [whispers], [laughs], [sighs]. In ChatGPT or Gemini you can just ask: "Say that again, slower and more excited."

This helps with reading a story to a child, practicing a hard conversation, or making a short video sound professional.

Try it: tap through the four readings. Notice that it is the same voice every time.

"I'm not mad. I just think you could've told me."

Copied voices and phone scams

Many voice tools can copy a real person's voice from a short recording. That helps people who are losing their voice to an illness, and creators who want to dub their videos into other languages.

Scammers use it too. They take a clip from a video someone posted online, copy the voice, and call a family member with a fake emergency.

How to protect your family:

  • Hang up and call the person back on a number you already know.
  • Agree on a family code word that a caller has to say.
  • Be very suspicious of anyone asking for gift cards, wire transfers or crypto, or asking you to keep it secret.

Try it: play the call. Then press "Show the warning signs".

"Grandma? Hey, it's... it's me.1 Yeah. Um, I'm okay, I'm okay, but I... I got in an accident and they're saying I have to pay bail before they let me go.2 Please don't tell Mom, she's gonna freak out.3 Can you, um... can you go get some gift cards?4 I'll explain everything later, I promise."
  • 1 No name. They wait for you to say it.
  • 2 Rushing you so you don't stop to check.
  • 3 Asking for secrecy, so nobody else can check either.
  • 4 Gift cards can't be traced or refunded. No real police or bail office takes them.

Talking to AI used to be a relay race

Until recently, talking with a voice assistant meant a chain of three separate programs. The first turned your speech into text. A chatbot wrote an answer. A third program read the answer out loud.

Each program had to wait for the program before it to finish, and the waits added up to long, awkward pauses. Only text was passed along, so your tone of voice got lost on the way.

Newer voice models do it all in a single step: sound in, sound out. In everyday conversation, people usually start answering about 0.2 seconds after the other person stops, and the newest models are getting close to that.

Try it: press Ask and watch the clocks.

You, sounding worried: "Is it going to rain on Saturday? It's my daughter's party."

Listening while it talks

Older voice assistants worked like a walkie-talkie: the two sides had to take turns. If you paused to think, they jumped in. If you tried to stop them, they couldn't hear you.

The newest models listen and speak at the same time, like a phone call. OpenAI's GPT-Live, which came out in July 2026, decides many times a second whether to keep talking, stop, wait, or say "mhmm". If you pause, it waits. If you interrupt, it stops and listens.

Try it: press Start and watch both. Halfway through the recipe, you cut in.

Older: walkie-talkie
New: listens while it talks

Thinking fast and slow

In his book Thinking, Fast and Slow, the psychologist Daniel Kahneman described two ways people think. Fast thinking is quick and automatic, like 2 + 2. Slow thinking takes effort, like 17 × 24, or planning a trip.

The newest voice AI copies this. A fast model stays in the conversation with you. It answers easy things right away and keeps the chat going. When you ask something hard, it hands the question to a slower thinking model in the background, then brings the answer back into the conversation when it's ready.

GPT-Live does this with GPT-5.5 Thinking. In ChatGPT you can pick Instant for quick answers, or Medium or High when you want it to think longer.

Try it: press Ask and compare the two.

Older: thinks in silence
New: fast and slow

Cleaning up a recording

Most recordings have unwanted sound in them: a fan, traffic, a hum from a cable, people talking at the next table.

The old way to clean it is a filter. Measure what the noise looks like on the spectrogram, then turn those pitches down everywhere. It helps, but it also takes a bite out of the voice.

AI cleanup tools learned from huge numbers of recordings, each with a clean and a noisy version. It's the same trick image generators use: add noise, then learn to remove it. They know what a voice should sound like, so they can rebuild the parts the noise covered up. Adobe Podcast's Enhance Speech is free to try.

Try it: press Play, then flip between noisy and filtered while it plays.

Making music

Music generators work the same way as AI voices: sound tokens, predicted in order, steered by your words. They learned from huge amounts of music paired with descriptions and lyrics.

A short request gets you the average. "A song" came back as upbeat pop. Every detail you add moves it further from average.

If you don't give it lyrics, it writes its own, and those are usually what gives an AI song away. The last step uses lyrics written by a person.

Try it: add details step by step and listen to how the song changes. Tap any step to go back to it.

Lyrics

AI songs are already on the charts

AI songs are already out in the world, and most people can't tell. In November 2025, an AI country act called Breaking Rust reached number 1 on a Billboard sales chart. A band called The Velvet Sundown built up a big following on Spotify before admitting the music was made by AI.

In a survey by the music app Deezer, 97% of the 9,000 people asked couldn't tell AI songs from songs made by people.

Record labels say these models were trained on their songs without permission, and they went to court. Some have since made deals with the AI companies, and others are still in court.

Your turn: make a song for someone

  1. Fill in the boxes on the right. The details are what make it yours.
